535.name: Heat ED visits, Number
535.indName: Heat stress: yearly emergency department visits
535.desc: ED visits due to heat-related illnesses, such as heat stroke and heat exhaustion. These represent part of the public health burden of extreme heat.
535.how: The number of NYC residents treated in a NYC emergency department (ED) during the months of May-September for the effects of heat and light due to weather conditions or undetermined cause. Residents with a diagnosis of excessive heat due to non-environmental conditions were excluded. Data are based on date of visit and include those with a diagnosis of heat-related illness, even if that was not the principal diagnosis. The data also include patients admitted to the hospital after being treated in an emergency department. Notes: The coding system used to represent diagnoses changed in October 2015. Cases occuring before October 1, 2015 are represented by International Classification of Diseases (ICD), 9th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) codes 992.0-992.9, E900.0 or E900.9. Cases admitted on or after October 1, 2015, are represented by the ICD, 10th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes T67, X30, X32. Cases with diagnoses represented by ICD-9-CM code E900.1 (if admitted before October 1, 2015) or ICD-10-CM code W92 (if admitted on or after October 1, 2015) were excluded. Because of the October 1, 2015 change in diagnostic codes from ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM, changes in numbers and rates over time should be interpreted with caution because they may be in part due to changes in the coding system.
535.src: New York State Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (SPARCS) Deidentified Hospital Discharge Data

643.name: Traffic, Million miles
643.desc: Annual vehicle miles travelled. Traffic density can influence health as a source of air pollution and traffic-related injuries.
643.how: The average number of vehicles traveling on a road segment on any given day during the year was estimated for each segment in a geography. The number of vehicles was multiplied by length of road segment to arrive at a daily vehicle-miles measure for that segment. The daily vehicle-miles measures were summed across all segments in a geography and then multiplied by 365 to arrive at an annual measure. Vehicle-miles are expressed in millions per square mile.

748.name: Cold hospitalizations, Age-adjusted rate
748.desc: Hospitalizations for cold-related illnesses, such as hypothermia and frostbite. These are part of the health burden of cold weather. Cold weather can also make chronic conditions worse.
748.how: NYC residents admitted to a NYC hospital during the months of October-April for the effects of reduced temperature or excessive or extreme cold due to weather conditions or undetermined cause (International Classification of Diseases, 9th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) codes 991, E901.0, E901.8, E901.9, or E988.3 if admitted before October 1, 2015; International Classification of Diseases, 10th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes X31, T68, T69, T33, T34 if admitted on or after October 1, 2015). Residents with a diagnostic code for excessive cold due to man-made conditions were excluded (ICD-9-CM code E901.1 if admitted before October 1, 2015; ICD-10-CM code W93 if admitted on or after October 1, 2015). Annual data is based on date of admission, and include those who were admitted with a diagnosis of cold-related illness in any principal or other diagnostic field. The data also include patients admitted to the hospital after being treated in an emergency department. Counts are summed by 5-year age groups and divided by the population in each age group, using NYC DOHMH intercensal estimates; quotients are multiplied by the proportion of the 2000 US population in each age group. Age-adjusted rate is the sum of the weighted age-specific rates; expressed as cases per 100,000 residents.
748.src: New York State Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (SPARCS) Deidentified Hospital Discharge Data; United States Census

1224.name: Park access, Percent
1224.desc: The percentage of the population who live within walking distance to a park: a quarter-mile or less to entrances of smaller sites, such as sitting areas and playgrounds, and half-mile or less to entrances of larger parks. Increased access to green space and open space can contribute to increased levels of physical activity.

1225.name: Unhealthy food access, Ratio
1225.desc: The ratio of bodegas to supermarkets. This can indicate whether the environment makes accessing unhealthy food easier for residents, as bodegas are less likely to have healthy food options than supermarkets.

Bodegas are defined as food purchasing establishments with less than 4,000 square foot and excludes specialty stores, such as bakeries and vitamin stores. Supermarkets are defined as retail food purchasing establishments with greater than or equal to 10,000 square feet or have a chain supermarket name regardless of size.
1225.src: NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets

1277.name: Fall-related ED visits, Rate
1277.indLabel: Fall-related emergency department visits among older adults
1277.desc: ED visits due to falls among people over age 65. Falls are a leading cause of injury among older adults.
1277.how:

Age-adjusted rates were calculated from number of non-fatal fall-related injury emergency department visits divided by the corresponding age-specific NYC DOHMH population estimates, modified from US Census Bureau interpolated intercensal population estimates, 2000-2021 (updated September 2022) and 2020-2023 (updated March 2025). Age-adjusted rate is the sum of these weighted rates, expressed as cases per 100,000 residents. Non-fatal fall-related injury emergency department visits were identified following the National Health Statistics Injury Framework for injury intent and mechanism classification using these first-listed external cause International Classification of Disease 10th Revision Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes: V00.11-V00.89 with 6th character=1; W00-W15, W17, W19; W16 with 6th character=2 (Except 16.4 and 16.9 with 5th character=2); W18.1, W18.2, W18.3 (National Center for Health Statistics). 1283.name: Heat hospitalizations, Average annual age-adjusted rate
1283.desc: Hospitalizations due to hot weather. These are part of the public health burden due to hot weather. Data aggregated over 10 years provides enough stablility to display neighborhood impacts.
1283.how: The number of NYC residents admitted to a NYC hospital during the months of May-September summed over a 10-year period for the effects of heat and light due to weather conditions or undetermined cause. Residents with a diagnosis of excessive heat due to non-environmental conditions were excluded. Data are based on date of admission and include those who were admitted with a diagnosis of heat-related illness, even if that was not the principal diagnosis. The data also include patients admitted to the hospital after being treated in an emergency department. Numbers are summed by 5-year age groups and divided by the population in each age group, using NYC DOHMH intercensal estimates. Quotients are multiplied by the proportion of the 2000 US population in each age group. The Average annual age-adjusted rate is the sum of the weighted age-specific rates; expressed as cases per 100,000 residents. Notes: The coding system used to represent diagnoses changed in October 2015. Cases admitted before October 1, 2015 are represented by International Classification of Diseases (ICD), 9th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) codes 992.0-992.9, E900.0 or E900.9. Cases admitted on or after October 1, 2015, are represented by the ICD, 10th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes T67, X30, X32. Cases with diagnoses represented by ICD-9-CM code E900.1 (if admitted before October 1, 2015) or ICD-10-CM code W92 (if admitted on or after October 1, 2015) were excluded. Because of the October 1, 2015 change in diagnostic codes from ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM, changes in numbers and rates over time should be interpreted with caution because they may be in part due to changes in the coding system.

1403.name: Heat stress: 5-year emergency department visits, Number
1403.desc: ED visits due to heat-related illnesses, such as heat stroke and heat exhaustion. These are part of the public health burden of extreme heat.
1403.how: The number of NYC residents treated in a NYC emergency department (ED) over 5 years during the months of May-September for the effects of heat and light due to weather conditions or undetermined cause. Residents with a diagnosis of excessive heat due to non-environmental conditions were excluded. Data are based on date of visit and include those with a diagnosis of heat-related illness, even if that was not the principal diagnosis. The data also include patients admitted to the hospital after being treated in an emergency department. Notes: The coding system used to represent diagnoses changed in October 2015. Cases occuring before October 1, 2015 are represented by International Classification of Diseases (ICD), 9th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) codes 992.0-992.9, E900.0 or E900.9. Cases admitted on or after October 1, 2015, are represented by the ICD, 10th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes T67, X30, X32. Cases with diagnoses represented by ICD-9-CM code E900.1 (if admitted before October 1, 2015) or ICD-10-CM code W92 (if admitted on or after October 1, 2015) were excluded. Because of the October 1, 2015 change in diagnostic codes from ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM, changes in numbers and rates over time should be interpreted with caution because they may be in part due to changes in the coding system.
